L306: Pairing codes expire after 1 hour, are rate-limited, and use cryptographic randomness.
L307: ### Admins vs Regular Userscite39†​ L308: 
L309: Allowlists answer "can this person reach the bot at all?" The admin / user split answers "now that they're in, what are they allowed to do?"
L310: 
L311: Every allowed user falls into one of two tiers per scope (DM vs group/channel):
L312:   * Admin — full access. Can run every registered slash command (built-in + plugin) and use every gated capability.
L313:   * Regular user — restricted access. Can chat with the agent normally, but can only run the slash commands you explicitly enable. The always-allowed floor is `/help` and `/whoami`.
L314: 
L315: The tiers are configured per platform and per scope. DM admin status does not imply group/channel admin status — each scope has its own admin list.
L316: What the tiers gate today: slash commands. The split runs through the live command registry, so it covers built-ins and plugin-registered commands without per-feature wiring. Plain chat is not affected — non-admins can still talk to the agent.
L317: What may be gated in the future: more capability surfaces (tool access, model switching, expensive operations) will hang off the same admin / user distinction as we add them. Configuring the split now means those future restrictions land cleanly without you having to re-model who's an admin.
L318: #### Configurationcite40†​ L319: 
L320:     `
L321: 
L322:     gateway:
L323: 
L324:       platforms:
L325: 
L326:         discord:
L327: 
L328:           extra:
L329: 
L330:             allow_from: ["111", "222", "333"]
L331: 
L332:             allow_admin_from: ["111"]                    # admins → all slash commands
L333: 
L334:             user_allowed_commands: [status, model]       # what non-admins may run
L335: 
L336:             # Optional: separate group/channel scope
L337: 
L338:             group_allow_admin_from: ["111"]
L339:             group_user_allowed_commands: [status]
L340: 
L341:     `
L342: Backward compat: if `allow_admin_from` is not set for a scope, the tier split is disabled for that scope and every allowed user has full access. Existing installs keep working with no changes — opt in when you want the distinction.
L343: #### Inspecting your accesscite41†​ L344: 
L345: Use `/whoami` from any platform to see the active scope, your tier (admin / user / unrestricted), and which slash commands you can run. When an admin list is configured, `/help` and `/commands` show a non-admin only the commands they can actually run (`/help`, `/whoami`, plus `user_allowed_commands`); admins see the full catalog. See the cite42†Telegram and cite43†Discord pages for platform-specific examples.
L346: ## Redirecting the Agentcite44†​ L347: 
L348: Send a message while the agent is working to correct the active turn:
L349:   * Model generation restarts with context — reasoning already shown and visible partial text are retained as an ordinary assistant checkpoint
L350:   * Completed work stays available — prior tool calls and results remain in the turn
L351:   * Running tools finish safely — the correction is applied at the next tool-result boundary instead of killing the tool
L352:   * `/stop` remains a hard stop — use it to cancel the active turn and foreground work
L353: ### Queue vs interrupt vs steer (busy-input mode)cite45†​ L354: 
L355: By default, messaging a busy agent redirects its active turn (a running foreground terminal command is moved to the background rather than killed, so your message is read immediately). Two other modes are available:
L356:   * `queue` — follow-up messages wait and run as the next turn after the current task finishes. Each follow-up (text, voice note, video, document) gets its own turn in arrival order; only a rapid photo burst is merged into one album turn.
L357:   * `steer` — follow-up messages are injected into the current run via `/steer`, arriving at the agent after the next tool call. No interrupt, no new turn. Falls back to `queue` behavior if the agent hasn't started yet.
L358: Gateway steers (including explicit `/steer`) and active-turn redirects carry the requesting event's available platform, chat, thread, sender, message, profile, and scope identifiers as per-message JSON context. With `privacy.redact_pii: true`, identifiers in this model-visible context are hashed on supported platforms, including alternate and parent identifiers; the original event identifiers remain internal for routing. Otherwise identifiers are preserved exactly.
L359: Neither mode changes the session's system prompt or chooses a fallback reply destination. The context is routing data, not authorization or a guarantee of automatic delivery.
L360: 
L361:     `
L362: 
L363:     display:
L364: 
L365:       busy_input_mode: steer   # or queue, or interrupt (default)
L366: 
L367:       busy_ack_enabled: true   # set to false to suppress the ⚡/⏳/⏩ chat reply entirely
L368: 
L369:       busy_text_debounce_seconds: 0.35   # quiet window before merged busy text is delivered
L370: 
L371:       busy_text_hard_cap_seconds: 1.0    # never hold merged busy text longer than this
L372: 
L373:     `
L374: All four keys are read from each profile's own `config.yaml`, so multiplexed profiles keep independent busy policies; there is no process-environment override.
L375: 
L376: The first time you message a busy agent on any platform, Hermes appends a one-line reminder to the busy-ack explaining the knob (`"💡 First-time tip — …"`). The reminder fires once per install — a flag under `onboarding.seen.busy_input_prompt` latches it. Delete that key to see the tip again.
L377: If you find the busy acknowledgment noisy, set `display.busy_ack_enabled: false`. Input handling is unchanged; only the confirmation message is hidden.
L378: ## Clarify Questions (Multi-Select)cite46†​ L379: 
L380: When the agent uses the `clarify` tool to ask you a question, the gateway renders the choices as a numbered prompt (or native buttons on platforms that support them). Clarify supports multi-select questions too — the agent can let you pick several options at once:
L381:   * Messaging platforms — the prompt says "Multiple selections allowed"; reply with the numbers separated by commas or spaces (e.g. `1, 3`), the option text, or your own free-form answer.
L382:   * Classic CLI / TUI — multi-select renders as checkboxes: Space toggles an option, Enter submits the selection.
L383: 
L384: Single-select prompts behave as before: pick one option by number, button, or text, or type your own answer via the "Other" path.
L385: ## Tool Progress Notificationscite47†​ L386: Control how much tool activity is displayed in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:

L389: 
L390:     display:
L391: 
L392:       tool_progress: all    # off | new | all | verbose | log
L393: 
L394:       tool_progress_command: false  # set to true to enable /verbose in messaging
L395:

L547: The unit Hermes installs already shuts the gateway down cleanly with `KillMode=mixed` + `KillSignal=SIGTERM`, and uses `Restart=always` with `RestartForceExitStatus` so updates and `/restart` respawn correctly. L558: The installed unit also maps `systemctl reload hermes-gateway` to `SIGUSR1`. L741: ### Automatic circuit breakercite66†​ L742: 
L743: Each adapter is wrapped in a circuit breaker. L420: ## Child Timeoutcite56†​ L421: 
L422: By default there is no wall-clock timeout on subagents. Children fail only from what they're actually doing — API errors, tool errors, or hitting their iteration budget — never from a delegation-level stopwatch. Earlier releases shipped a hard cap (300s, later 600s), which kept killing legitimately busy children mid-task: deep code reviews, large research fan-outs, and slow reasoning models routinely need more than 10 minutes while making steady progress the whole time.
L424: A child whose progress is completely frozen past the stale threshold — 450s idle between turns, 1200s while inside a tool — is interrupted and its wait is abandoned: the parent gets a `status: "timeout"` entry whose error reads `Subagent stopped making progress after N API call(s) — no activity for 450s (heartbeat stale threshold); the pending worker was abandoned.` The wait ends even in one-shot runs (`hermes chat -Q`, Bot Chat one-shot, cron) that have no gateway inactivity watchdog behind them, so a wedged child can no longer hold the turn or its session lease forever.
L425: An in-flight model wait still counts as progress — subagents refresh the activity clock while waiting on the provider, so a slow local / long-prefill completion is not treated as stalled.
L426: If you want a cap anyway (e.g. cost control on unattended cron-driven delegation), opt in per-install:
L427: 
L428:     `
L429: 
L430:     delegation:
L431: 
L432:       child_timeout_seconds: 0     # default: 0 = no timeout
L433: 
L434:       # child_timeout_seconds: 1800  # opt-in inactivity cap (floor 30s)
L435: 
L436:     `
L437: A positive value bounds inactivity, not total runtime: it is the longest a child may go with no progress (no completed API call, no tool change, no activity-clock tick) before it is abandoned. Every sign of progress restarts the window, so a child waiting on a multi-minute completion — the case that used to lose finished work — is never killed for taking long, while a child that has genuinely stopped moving is still caught (and an in-flight request is bounded independently by the per-call stale watchdog).
L438: `0` or a negative value disables the cap; the heartbeat staleness monitor below stays active either way.
L439: At ~80% of an idle window the child receives a one-line `[delegation budget warning]` through its steer channel (delivered at its next iteration boundary) telling it how long it has been idle and to return its summary now, so a slow-but-recoverable child can wrap up instead of losing its context. The warning fires once per idle window and re-arms when progress resumes.
L440: When a configured cap or the stale threshold fires, the child's result carries structured timeout metadata alongside the error message so parents and hooks can distinguish a stopwatch kill from other failures without parsing text: `timeout_seconds` (whichever limit actually ended the wait — the stale threshold when it pre-empts a longer configured cap, otherwise the cap), `timed_out_after_seconds` (actual wall clock), `last_event_age` (how long the child had been silent when the wait ended — the fast way to tell a slow provider from a runaway), and `timeout_phase` (`before_first_llm_call` when the child never reached its first request, `after_llm_calls` otherwise).
L441: All four are `null` on non-timeout errors.
L442: ## Failure Visibilitycite57†​ L443: 
L444: A subagent that fails — non-retryable provider error (404/400), timeout, crash, or no usable output — is never silent:
L445:   * CLI: the delegation tree prints a one-line reason: `⚠️ Subagent failed — "your goal": HTTP 404: model not found (after 12s)`. Batch runs append the reason to the per-task `✗` completion line.
L446:   * Gateway platforms (Telegram, Discord, Slack, ...): the same clean line is delivered as a standalone chat notice, even when `tool_progress` is off for that platform.
L447:   * Parent agent: the tool result entry carries `status: "failed"` plus the full `error` text, so the model can react (retry, re-route, report).
L448: Error text is reduced to the single most informative line (the exception message, not a traceback wall) and capped in length.
L449: 
L450: Diagnostic dump on zero-call timeout
L451: With a hard cap configured, if a subagent times out having made zero API calls (usually: provider unreachable, auth failure, or tool-schema rejection), `delegate_task` writes a structured diagnostic to `~/.hermes/logs/subagent-timeout-<session>-<timestamp>.log` containing the subagent's config snapshot, credential-resolution trace, any early error messages, and stack traces for all live threads (not just the child's own) — a child parked waiting on a nested helper thread is indistinguishable from a slow provider without the full picture.
L452: ## Stall Detection for Background Subagentscite58†​ L453: 
L454: Background delegations (`delegate_task(background=true)`) are watched by a progress-based stall monitor — on by default, zero config. Unlike a wall-clock timeout, it never touches a child that is making progress, no matter how long it runs.
L455: The monitor samples each detached child's progress signals — API-call count, current tool, and last-activity timestamp (which ticks on every streamed token, tool transition, and API-call boundary, so a child mid-stream on a long response always counts as alive):
L456:   1. Progressing children are never touched. Any advancing signal resets the clock.
L457:   2. A child whose progress is completely frozen past the stale threshold (450s idle, 1200s while inside a tool — legitimately slow terminal commands and web fetches get the higher ceiling) is interrupted and given a 120s grace window. A child that unwinds in time delivers its partial results through the normal completion path.
L458:   3. A child that never returns is force-finalized with a terminal `stalled` completion event, so the owning session hears an outcome instead of going silent, and the async slot frees for new work.
L459: The `stalled` event carries structured metadata mirroring the sync-path timeout fields: `stalled_after_quiet_seconds`, `stall_threshold_seconds`, `stall_phase` (`idle` / `in_tool`), and `stall_grace_seconds`.

The underlying wedge (children hanging at their first API call after multi-day gateway uptime) was also fixed at the root: delegated children now run their OpenAI-wire API requests inline on their own conversation thread instead of a nested worker thread — the layer where the wedge lived. The stall monitor remains as the safety net for anything else.
L461: ## Monitoring Running Subagents (`/agents`)cite59†​ L462: 
L463: The TUI ships a `/agents` overlay (alias `/tasks`) that turns recursive `delegate_task` fan-out into a first-class audit surface:
L464:   * Live tree view of running and recently-finished subagents, grouped by parent
L465:   * Per-branch cost, token, and file-touched rollups
L466:   * Kill and pause controls — cancel a specific subagent mid-flight without interrupting its siblings
L467:   * Post-hoc review: step through each subagent's turn-by-turn history even after they've returned to the parent
L468: ### Live activity above the composercite60†​ L469: 
L470: The classic CLI, TUI, and Desktop automatically show live subagents above the composer. You can keep writing while watching the live count, task names, elapsed time, and latest activity. The terminal dock limits visible rows according to screen height and shows how many additional workers are hidden; Desktop previews up to three workers.

L758: For multi-bot Slack deployments that rely on strict per-turn mentions, keep the following profile:
L759:

L761:

L763: 
L764:       require_mention: true
L765: 
L766:       strict_mention: true
L767: 
L768:       allow_bots: mentions
L769: 
L770:       allowed_channels: ""
L771: 
L772:     `

L774: After gateway config changes, deploys, or restarts, run this synthetic smoke target:
L775: 
L776:     `
L777: 
L778:     scripts/run_tests.sh tests/gateway/test_slack_peer_agent_smoke.py -q
L779: 
L780:     `
L781: This target uses in-process synthetic Slack events only. It does not send live Slack messages and does not require real bot tokens by default.
L782: 
L783: Failure buckets:
L784:   * `config:` `test_peer_agent_smoke_preflight_contract` caught a profile mismatch (`require_mention`, `strict_mention`, `allow_bots`, or `allowed_channels`).
L785:   * `platform_connectivity:` the adapter/client was not initialized, so routing smoke is not a trustworthy signal yet.
L786:   * `bot_identity:` the adapter never resolved its bot user ID, so current-message mention checks cannot work.
L787:   * `routing_logic:` the Slack adapter regressed on one of the peer-agent invariants (human mention routing, peer-bot ignore, explicit peer mention admit, or passive ack/status/error suppression).

L789: ### Channel allowlist (`allowed_channels`)cite64†​ L790: 
L791: Restrict the bot to a fixed set of Slack channels — useful when the bot is invited to many channels but should only respond in a few. When set, messages from channels NOT in this list are silently ignored, even if the bot is `@mentioned`.
L792: 1:1 DMs are exempt from this filter, so authorized users can always reach the bot in a direct message. Group DMs (MPIMs) are not exempt — like channels, an MPIM must be on the allowlist (its ID starts with `G`) or its messages are dropped.
L793: 
L794:     `
L795: 
L796:     slack:
L797: 
L798:       allowed_channels:
L799: 
L800:         - "C0123456789"   # #ops
L801: 
L802:         - "C0987654321"   # #incident-response
L803: 
L804:     `
L805: Or via env var (comma-separated):
L806: 
L807:     `
L808: 
L809:     SLACK_ALLOWED_CHANNELS="C0123456789,C0987654321"

L811:     `

L813: Behavior:

L815:   * Empty / unset → no restriction (fully backward compatible).
L816:   * Non-empty → channel ID must be on the list, or the message is dropped before any other gating (mention requirement, `free_response_channels`, etc.) runs.

L260: # Hermes Agent ☤
L261: 
L262: cite173†Hermes Agent†hermes-agent.nousresearch.com | cite173†Hermes Desktop†hermes-agent.nousresearch.com L263: The self-improving AI agent built by cite174†Nous Research†nousresearch.com . It's the only agent with a built-in learning loop — it creates skills from experience, improves them during use, nudges itself to persist knowledge, searches its own past conversations, and builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions. Run it on a $5 VPS, a GPU cluster, or serverless infrastructure that costs nearly nothing when idle. It's not tied to your laptop — talk to it from Telegram while it works on a cloud VM.
L264: Use any model you want — cite175†Nous Portal†portal.nousresearch.com , OpenRouter, OpenAI, your own endpoint, and cite176†many others†hermes-agent.nousresearch.com . Switch with `hermes model` — no code changes, no lock-in.
L265: A real terminal interface  | Full TUI with multiline editing, slash-command autocomplete, conversation history, interrupt-and-redirect, and streaming tool output.
L266: Lives where you do  | Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and CLI — all from a single gateway process. Voice memo transcription, cross-platform conversation continuity.
L267: A closed learning loop  | Agent-curated memory with periodic nudges. Autonomous skill creation after complex tasks. Skills self-improve during use. FTS5 session search with LLM summarization for cross-session recall. cite177†Honcho dialectic user modeling. Compatible with the cite178†agentskills.io†agentskills.io open standard.
L268: Scheduled automations  | Built-in cron scheduler with delivery to any platform. Daily reports, nightly backups, weekly audits — all in natural language, running unattended.
L269: Delegates and parallelizes  | Spawn isolated subagents for parallel workstreams. Write Python scripts that call tools via RPC, collapsing multi-step pipelines into zero-context-cost turns.
L270: Runs anywhere, not just your laptop  | Seven terminal backends — local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona, and Vercel Sandbox. Daytona and Modal offer serverless persistence — your agent's environment hibernates when idle and wakes on demand, costing nearly nothing between sessions. Run it on a $5 VPS or a GPU cluster.
L271: Research-ready  | Batch trajectory generation, trajectory compression for training the next generation of tool-calling models.
L272: * * *
L273: ## Quick Install
L274: 
L275: ### Linux, macOS, WSL2
L276: 
L277:     curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash
L278: ### Windows (native, PowerShell)
L279: 
L280: > Heads up: Native Windows runs Hermes without WSL — CLI, gateway, TUI, and tools all work natively. If you'd rather use WSL2, the Linux/macOS one-liner above works there too. Found a bug? Please cite64†file issues .
L281: 
L282: Run this in PowerShell:
L283: 
L284:     iex (irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1)
L285: The source installer delegates Python 3.14, Node.js, npm, ripgrep, FFmpeg, and Python dependencies to PM. If Git is absent, it stages the verified Git for Windows archive in Hermes' tool store. It does not replace your system Git. See cite179†installation methods†hermes-agent.nousresearch.com for the separate MSIX/App Installer package and its update ownership.
L286: > Android / Termux: A signed APT repository is available for aarch64 devices, with a `stable` channel (tagged releases) and a prerelease `canary` channel. The package includes Python, Node.js, and the TUI. Use the cite180†Termux guide†hermes-agent.nousresearch.com , not the desktop/server installer script.
L287: >
L288: > Windows: Native Windows is fully supported — the PowerShell one-liner above installs everything. If you'd rather use WSL2, the Linux command works there too. Native Windows install lives under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes`; WSL2 installs under `~/.hermes` as on Linux.
L289: After installation:
L290: 
L291:     source ~/.bashrc    # reload shell (or: source ~/.zshrc)
L292:     hermes              # start chatting!
L293: ### Troubleshooting
L294: #### Windows Defender or antivirus flags `uv.exe` as malware
L295: 
L296: If your antivirus (Bitdefender, Windows Defender, etc.) quarantines `uv.exe` from the Hermes `bin` folder (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\bin\uv.exe`), this is a false positive. The file is Astral's `uv` — the Rust Python package manager Hermes bundles to manage its Python environment. ML-based antivirus engines commonly flag unsigned Rust binaries that download and install packages.
L297: To verify your copy is authentic:
L298: 
L299:     # Install GitHub CLI if needed
L300:     winget install --id GitHub.cli
L301: 
L302:     # Login to GitHub
L303:     gh auth login
L304: 
L305:     # Run verification
L306:     $uv = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\hermes\bin\uv.exe"
L307:     $ver = (& $uv --version).Split(' ')[1]
L308:     [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12
L309:     $zip = "$env:TEMP\uv.zip"
L310:     Invoke-WebRequest "https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases/download/$ver/uv-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip" -OutFile $zip -UseBasicParsing
L311:     gh attestation verify $zip --repo astral-sh/uv
L312:     Expand-Archive $zip "$env:TEMP\uv_x" -Force
L313:     (Get-FileHash "$env:TEMP\uv_x\uv.exe").Hash -eq (Get-FileHash $uv).Hash
L314: If attestation says "Verification succeeded" and the last line prints `True`, you're good.
L315: 
L316: To whitelist Hermes:
L317: 
L318:   * Windows Defender: Run PowerShell as Admin → `Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\hermes\bin"`
L319:   * Bitdefender: Add an exception in the Bitdefender console (Protection > Antivirus > Settings > Manage Exceptions)
L320:   * Whitelist the folder, not the file hash — Hermes updates `uv` and the hash changes every version
L321: For more context, see the upstream Astral reports: cite181†astral-sh/uv#13553 , cite182†astral-sh/uv#15011 , cite183†astral-sh/uv#10079 .

L324: ## Getting Started
L325: 
L326:     hermes              # Interactive CLI — start a conversation
L327:     hermes model        # Choose your LLM provider and model
L328:     hermes tools        # Configure which tools are enabled

L338: * * *
L339: ## Skip the API-key collection — Nous Portal
L340: 
L341: Hermes works with whatever provider you want — that's not changing. But if you'd rather not collect five separate API keys for the model, web search, image generation, TTS, and a cloud browser, cite175†Nous Portal†portal.nousresearch.com covers all of them under one subscription:
L342:   * 300+ models — pick any of them with `/model <name>`
L343:   * Tool Gateway — web search, image generation (FAL), text-to-speech (OpenAI), cloud browser (Browser Use), all routed through your sub. No extra accounts.
L344: 
L345: One command from a fresh install:
L346: 
L347:     hermes setup --portal
L348: 
L349: That logs you in via OAuth, sets Nous as your provider, and turns on the Tool Gateway. Check what's wired up any time with `hermes portal info`. Full details on the cite185†Tool Gateway docs page†hermes-agent.nousresearch.com .
L350: You can still bring your own keys per-tool whenever you want — the gateway is per-backend, not all-or-nothing.
L351: 
L352: * * *
L353: ## CLI vs Messaging Quick Reference
L354: 
L355: Hermes has two entry points: start the terminal UI with `hermes`, or run the gateway and talk to it from Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, or Email. Once you're in a conversation, many slash commands are shared across both interfaces.
L356: Action  | CLI  | Messaging platforms
L357: --- | --- | ---
L358: Start chatting  | `hermes`  | Run `hermes gateway setup` + `hermes gateway start`, then send the bot a message
L359: Start fresh conversation  | `/new` or `/reset`  | `/new` or `/reset`
L360: Change model  | `/model [provider:model]`  | `/model [provider:model]`
L361: Set a personality  | `/personality [name]`  | `/personality [name]`
L362: Retry or undo the last turn  | `/retry`, `/undo`  | `/retry`, `/undo`
L363: Compress context / check usage  | `/compress`, `/usage`, `/insights [--days N]`  | `/compress`, `/usage`, `/insights [days]`
L364: Browse skills  | `/skills` or `/<skill-name>`  | `/<skill-name>`
L365: Interrupt current work  | `Ctrl+C` or send a new message  | `/stop` or send a new message
L366: Platform-specific status  | `/platforms`  | `/status`, `/sethome`
L367: For the full command lists, see the cite186†CLI guide†hermes-agent.nousresearch.com and the cite187†Messaging Gateway guide†hermes-agent.nousresearch.com .

36:         ("slack_sdk", slack_sdk),
37:         ("slack_sdk.web", slack_sdk.web),
38:         ("slack_sdk.web.async_client", slack_sdk.web.async_client),
39:     ]:
40:         sys.modules.setdefault(name, mod)
41: 
42: 
43: _ensure_slack_mock()
44:

46: 
47: _slack_mod.SLACK_AVAILABLE = True
48:

With a hard cap configured, if a subagent times out having made zero API calls (usually: provider unreachable, auth failure, or tool-schema rejection), `delegate_task` writes a structured diagnostic to `~/.hermes/logs/subagent-timeout-<session>-<timestamp>.log` containing the subagent's config snapshot, credential-resolution trace, any early error messages, and stack traces for all live threads (not just the child's own) — a child parked waiting on a nested helper thread is indistinguishable from a slow provider without the full picture.
## Inherited Tool Access​

`delegate_task` does not accept a model-facing `toolsets` parameter. Each subagent inherits the parent's enabled toolsets so the model cannot grant a child capabilities that the parent does not have. Configure the parent's tools before starting the conversation if delegated work needs additional capabilities.

Certain tools are blocked for subagents even when the parent has them:

  * `delegate_task` — blocked for leaf subagents (the default). Retained for `role="orchestrator"` children, bounded by `max_spawn_depth` — see Depth Limit and Nested Orchestration below.
  * `clarify` — subagents cannot interact with the user
  * `memory` — no writes to shared persistent memory
  * `send_message` — no cross-platform side effects
  * `cronjob` — no scheduling more work in the parent's name

Both roles retain `execute_code` (programmatic tool calling) so children can batch mechanical work.

## Max Iterations​

Each subagent has an iteration limit (default: 250) that controls how many tool-calling turns it can take. The limit is set globally in `config.yaml` and applies to every child; it is not a per-call parameter of `delegate_task`:
    
    `
    
    # In ~/.hermes/config.yaml
    
    delegation:
    
      max_iterations: 60   # lower it for fleets of simple tasks, raise it for long investigations
    
    `

A child that exhausts its budget returns with `exit_reason: max_iterations` and `truncated: true`, so the parent can tell a budget stop from a completed task.

## Child Timeout​

By default there is no wall-clock timeout on subagents. Children fail only from what they're actually doing — API errors, tool errors, or hitting their iteration budget — never from a delegation-level stopwatch. Earlier releases shipped a hard cap (300s, later 600s), which kept killing legitimately busy children mid-task: deep code reviews, large research fan-outs, and slow reasoning models routinely need more than 10 minutes while making steady progress the whole time.

Genuinely stuck children are still detected: the heartbeat staleness monitor stops refreshing the parent's activity when a child makes no progress (no API calls, no tool starts, and no activity-timestamp ticks), letting the gateway inactivity timeout fire on a truly wedged worker. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

General rules for all hooks:

  * Callbacks receive keyword arguments. Always accept `**kwargs` for forward compatibility.
  * Callback exceptions are logged and skipped; later callbacks continue. A callback that fails the same way on every call (typically a signature naming a field the hook does not send, e.g. `tool_data` instead of `tool_name`/`args`) is reported once at WARNING — the message lists the fields the hook provides — and identical repeats go to DEBUG, so a mis-declared plugin cannot flood the log.
  * If a Python plugin callback on a timeout-bounded hook (hot-path observers such as `post_tool_call` / `pre_llm_call`, plus the policy hook `pre_tool_call`) blocks longer than `plugins.hook_callback_timeout` (default 30s, set `0` to disable, max 600), it is abandoned without joining the worker so the agent loop continues. Timed-out or still-running `pre_tool_call` callbacks fail closed (block the tool); other bounded hooks fail open (skip). 
Set `fail_closed: true` (or `failClosed: true`, the Cursor/Claude Code spelling) on a `pre_tool_call` entry to invert that:
    
    `
    
    hooks:
    
      pre_tool_call:
    
        - matcher: "terminal|write_file|patch"
    
          command: "~/.hermes/agent-hooks/secret-scan.sh"
    
          timeout: 10
    
          fail_closed: true
    
    `

With `fail_closed: true`, each of these now blocks the tool call with `hook <command> failed closed: <reason>`:

Failure  | Fail-open (default)  | `fail_closed: true`
--- | --- | ---
Command not found / not executable  | warn, proceed  | block
Timeout  | warn, proceed  | block
Non-JSON stdout (e.g. a stack trace)  | warn, proceed  | block
Clean exit, valid no-op JSON (`{}`)  | proceed  | proceed

`fail_closed` only applies to blocking-capable events (`pre_tool_call` today); setting it on any other event logs a warning at config-parse time and is ignored. `hermes hooks test` reflects these semantics — the `parsed` line shows exactly the block shape the dispatcher would receive.
    
          events: [on_session_end, subagent_stop]
    
          secret_env: HERMES_OUTBOUND_WEBHOOK_SECRET   # env var holding the HMAC secret
    
          timeout: 10                           # per-attempt seconds (1–60)
    
        - name: tool-monitor
    
          url: https://metrics.example.com/hooks/hermes
    
          events: [post_tool_call]
    
          matcher: "terminal|delegate_task"     # regex, tool-scoped events only
    
    `

Any event from the plugin-hook set is valid (`pre_tool_call`, `post_tool_call`, `pre_llm_call`, `post_llm_call`, `on_session_start`, `on_session_end`, `subagent_start`, `subagent_stop`, ...). Malformed entries warn and are skipped — a broken webhook never crashes the agent. Changes take effect on the next CLI session / gateway restart.

Secrets: prefer `secret_env` (the name of an environment variable, typically set in `~/.hermes/.env`) over an inline `secret:` literal, so the config file stays free of credentials. Entries without a secret are delivered unsigned (flagged as `UNSIGNED` by `hermes hooks list`).

L61: ## Quick startcite35†​ L62: 
L63: If this is your first time running Hermes Agent, create a data directory on the host and start the container interactively to run the setup wizard:

L65: Avoid browser-based VPS consoles for the install commands
L66: Some VPS providers (Hetzner Cloud, and several others) offer a browser-based console for managing hosts. L70: 
L71:     mkdir -p ~/.hermes
L72:

L74: 
L75:       -v ~/.hermes:/opt/data \

L77:       nousresearch/hermes-agent setup
L78: 
L79:     `

L601: ## Resource limitscite55†​ L602: 
L603: The Hermes container needs moderate resources. Recommended minimums:
L604: 
L605: Resource  | Minimum  | Recommended
L606: --- | --- | ---
L607: Memory  | 1 GB  | 2–4 GB
L608: CPU  | 1 core  | 2 cores
L609: Disk (data volume)  | 500 MB  | 2+ GB (grows with sessions/skills)
L610: 
L611: Browser automation (Playwright/Chromium) is the most memory-hungry feature. If you don't need browser tools, 1 GB is sufficient. With browser tools active, allocate at least 2 GB.
L612: Set limits in Docker:
L613: 
L614:     `
L615: 
L616:     docker run -d \
L617: 
L618:       --name hermes \
L619: 
L620:       --restart unless-stopped \
L621: 
L622:       --memory=4g --cpus=2 \
L623: 
L624:       -v ~/.hermes:/opt/data \
L625: 
L626:       nousresearch/hermes-agent gateway run
L627: 
L628:     `
L629: ## What the Dockerfile doescite56†​ L630: 
L631: The image uses Debian 13.4 and includes:
L632:   * A Python 3.14 environment synchronized from the committed `uv.lock`, followed by a no-dependency editable install of Hermes.
L633:   * The curated extras `all`, `messaging`, `otlp`, `anthropic`, `bedrock`, `azure-identity`, and `matrix`. This is not `--all-extras`.
L634:   * Node.js 26 and npm from the digest-pinned Node source image.
L635:   * PM-pinned uv, full Chromium, FFmpeg, and ripgrep in `/opt/hermes/tools`.
L636:   * System Git, OpenSSH, Docker CLI, and Chromium shared libraries.
L637:   * Prebuilt TUI/dashboard assets and baked Photon sidecar dependencies.
L638:   * s6-overlay for supervision and zombie-process cleanup.
L639: Chromium is staged through PM, not `npx playwright install`. The build records its resolved executable in `/etc/hermes/agent-browser-executable-path`. `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` names `/opt/hermes/tools`, outside the data mount.
L640: Every image, including the unsuffixed (non-`-desktop`) tags, carries the full Chromium build rather than Playwright's lighter headless shell: one pinned, checksummed browser serves both headless browsing and headed Bot Screen sessions. The cost is image size — the full build is larger than the headless shell earlier images shipped.
L641: Opt-in backend SDKs (Edge TTS, Firecrawl, Exa, platform adapters, plugin dependencies) install on first use into PM dependency generations under `/opt/data/installs`, so they survive container recreation and image updates. The image's own `/opt/hermes/.venv` is never modified.
L642: On each boot the container re-resolves the recorded selection against the new image's lock before services start; if that fails (for example offline), it boots the image's own environment and keeps the recorded extras for the next boot or install. Set `security.allow_lazy_installs: false` to refuse on-demand installs. The old `lazy-packages` overlay is not used.
L643: Image provenance lives at `/etc/hermes/image-provenance.json`, outside both the source and data mounts. The build stamp lives at `/opt/hermes/install-stamp.json`. A local build without a supplied stamp reports an unknown revision rather than inventing a commit. `hermes update` refuses image-owned code changes; replace the image to update the application.

L398: ### Restart-safe workers under systemdcite57†​ L399: 
L400: When the gateway runs as a systemd service, each due job is handed to an external worker process launched in a transient user scope (`systemd-run --user --scope`), so restarting the gateway mid-job does not kill the job. Creating that scope needs a user systemd session; hosts without one (containers, minimal LXCs, a service user without linger) cannot provide it.
L401: By default cron then degrades: the job still runs as a separate external process with the same execution handoff, but without cgroup isolation, so a gateway restart during the job kills it (the execution ledger records that). One warning is logged per gateway process. To fail closed instead — skip the job and record the error on the job row — set:
L402: 
L403:     `
L404: 
L405:     cron:
L406: 
L407:       require_restart_safe_scope: true
L408: 
L409:     `

L681: ## Script timeoutcite77†​ L682: 
L683: Pre-run scripts (attached via the `script` parameter) have a default timeout of 3600 seconds (1 hour). This bounds the script only — skill-based / LLM-driven jobs run on a separate inactivity budget and are not capped by this value. If your scripts need a different limit, you can change it:
L684: 
L685:     `
L686: 
L687:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L688: 
L689:     cron:
L690: 
L691:       script_timeout_seconds: 1800   # 30 minutes
L692: 
L693:     `
L694: Or set the `HERMES_CRON_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT` environment variable. The resolution order is: env var → config.yaml → 3600s default.
L695: Cron also bounds post-run session and agent-resource cleanup. This happens after the LLM turn returns, so it is separate from the inactivity timeout. The default is 10 seconds per cleanup operation. If a storage or client finalizer stops returning, the scheduler logs an error, releases the job's in-flight guard, and allows later runs to dispatch instead of skipping that job forever.
L696: 
L697:     `
L698: 
L699:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L700: 
L701:     cron:
L702: 
L703:       cleanup_timeout_seconds: 10
L704: 
L705:     `
L706: Set `cleanup_timeout_seconds: 0` only to restore the legacy unbounded cleanup behavior.
L707: ## Media send timeoutcite78†​ L708: 
L709: When a cron delivery includes media attachments (a generated PDF, TTS audio, an exported report) sent through a live gateway adapter, each attachment upload is bounded by a timeout — 300 seconds by default. Large files on slow uplinks can need more:
L710: 
L711:     `
L712: 
L713:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L714: 
L715:     cron:
L716: 
L717:       media_send_timeout_seconds: 600   # 10 minutes per attachment
L718: 
L719:     `
L720: Or set the `HERMES_CRON_MEDIA_SEND_TIMEOUT` environment variable. The resolution order is: env var → config.yaml → 300s default. A timed-out attachment is recorded in the job's run status as a partial delivery failure (the text still delivers).
L721: ## Bot Chat delivery timeoutcite79†​ L722: 
L723: A `bot-chat` delivery runs a full agent turn in the target bot's chat, so its bound is minutes, not seconds — 600s by default:
L724: 
L725:     `
L726: 
L727:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L728: 
L729:     cron:
L730: 
L731:       bot_chat_delivery_timeout_seconds: 900
L732: 
L733:     `
L734: 
L735: A timed-out delivery is recorded in `last_delivery_error`; the bot's turn may still complete on its own.
L736: The cap bounds the bot's turn only. When that turn messages a teammate (`message_agent`), the delivery process stays alive afterwards — bounded by `terminal.oneshot_completion_wait_seconds` — so the teammate's reply can land in the Bot Chat; that wait is not part of the delivery and is never counted against, or cut short by, this cap.
L737: ## Standalone send timeoutcite80†​ L738: 
L739: When the live gateway adapter cannot deliver (or no gateway is running), a target is sent through the platform's standalone sender. That send is bounded by a wall-clock timeout — 60 seconds by default — so a transport that is mid-reconnect cannot pin the job run (and a pending restart drain behind it) indefinitely:
L740: 
L741:     `
L742: 
L743:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L744: 
L745:     cron:
L746: 
L747:       standalone_send_timeout_seconds: 120
L748: 
L749:     `
L750: A timed-out send is recorded in `last_delivery_error` as `standalone send to <target> timed out after Ns`; the message may still land if the adapter had already accepted it.
L751: ## No-agent mode (script-only jobs)cite32†​ L752: 
L753: For recurring jobs that don't need LLM reasoning — classic watchdogs, disk/memory alerts, heartbeats, CI pings — pass `no_agent=True` at creation time. The scheduler runs your script on schedule and delivers its stdout directly, skipping the agent entirely:
L754: 
L755:     `
L756: 
L757:     hermes cron create "every 5m" \
L758: 
L759:       --no-agent \
L760: 
L761:       --script memory-watchdog.sh \
L762: 
L763:       --deliver telegram \
L764: 
L765:       --name "memory-watchdog"
L766: 
L767:     `
L768: 
L769: Semantics:
L770:   * Script stdout (trimmed) → delivered verbatim as the message.
L771:   * Empty stdout → silent tick, no delivery. This is the watchdog pattern: "only say something when something is wrong".
L772:   * Non-zero exit or timeout → an error alert is delivered, so a broken watchdog can't fail silently.
L773:   * `{"wakeAgent": false}` on the last line → silent tick (same gate LLM jobs use).
L774:   * No tokens, no model, no provider fallback — the job never touches the inference layer.
L775: `.sh` / `.bash` files run under `bash` from `PATH` when available, otherwise `/bin/bash` (important on Windows Git Bash). Anything else runs under the current Python interpreter (`sys.executable`). Scripts must resolve inside `$HERMES_HOME/scripts/` — relative names, absolute paths, and `~`-prefixed paths are accepted when the resolved target stays in that directory; paths that escape it are rejected.

L38: # Slack Setup
L39: 
L40: Connect Hermes Agent to Slack as a bot using Socket Mode. Socket Mode uses WebSockets instead of public HTTP endpoints, so your Hermes instance doesn't need to be publicly accessible — it works behind firewalls, on your laptop, or on a private server.
L41: 
L42: Classic Slack Apps Deprecated
L43: 
L44: Classic Slack apps (using RTM API) were fully deprecated in March 2025. Hermes uses the modern Bolt SDK with Socket Mode. If you have an old classic app, you must create a new one following the steps below.
L45: ## Overviewcite23†​ L46: 
L47: Component  | Value
L48: --- | ---
L49: Library  | `slack-bolt` / `slack_sdk` for Python (Socket Mode)
L50: Connection  | WebSocket — no public URL required
L51: Auth tokens needed  | Bot Token (`xoxb-`) + App-Level Token (`xapp-`)
L52: User identification  | Slack Member IDs (e.g., `U01ABC2DEF3`)
L53: 
L54: * * *
L55: ## Step 1: Create a Slack Appcite24†​ L56: 
L57: The fastest path is to paste a manifest Hermes generates for you. It declares every built-in slash command (`/btw`, `/stop`, `/model`, …), every required OAuth scope, every event subscription, and enables Socket Mode — all at once.
L58: ### Option A: From a Hermes-generated manifest (recommended)cite25†​ L59: 
L60:   1. Generate the manifest. New Slack apps must use Agent view:
L61: 
L62:     `
L63: 
L64:     hermes slack manifest --agent-view --write
L65: 
L66:     `
L67: 
L68: This writes `~/.hermes/slack-manifest.json` and prints paste-in instructions. Existing apps that still use Slack's legacy Assistant view can omit `--agent-view` until they are ready to migrate.
L69: To populate Slack's long app description from an existing UTF-8 text or Markdown file, add `--long-description-file`:
L70: 
L71:     `
L72: 
L73:     hermes slack manifest --agent-view \
L74: 
L75:       --long-description-file AGENTS.md --write
L76: 
L77:     `
L78: 
L79: The file contents are preserved exactly within Slack's 175–4,000-character range. Use `--long-description "..."` for inline text instead; the inline and file options are mutually exclusive and cannot be combined with `--slashes-only`.
L80:   2. Go to cite26†https://api.slack.com/apps†api.slack.com → Create New App → From an app manifest
L81: 
L82:   3. Pick your workspace, paste the JSON contents, review, click Next → Create
L83: 
L84:   4. Skip ahead to Step 6: Install App to Workspace. The manifest handled scopes, events, and slash commands for you.
L85: ### Option B: From scratch (manual)cite27†​ L86: 
L87:   1. Go to cite26†https://api.slack.com/apps†api.slack.com L88:   2. Click Create New App
L89:   3. Choose From scratch
L90:   4. Enter an app name (e.g., "Hermes Agent") and select your workspace
L91:   5. Click Create App
L92: 
L93: You'll land on the app's Basic Information page. Continue with Steps 2–6 below.
L94: 
L95: * * *
L124: ## Step 3: Enable Socket Modecite29†​ L125: 
L126: Socket Mode lets the bot connect via WebSocket instead of requiring a public URL.
L127: 
L128:   1. In the sidebar, go to Settings → Socket Mode
L129:   2. Toggle Enable Socket Mode to ON
L130:   3. You'll be prompted to create an App-Level Token:
L131:      * Name it something like `hermes-socket` (the name doesn't matter)
L132:      * Add the `connections:write` scope
L133:      * Click Generate
L134:   4. Copy the token — it starts with `xapp-`. This is your `SLACK_APP_TOKEN`
L135: 
L136: tip
L260: Under the hood: Hermes ships with a generated Slack app manifest (see Step 1, Option A) that declares every command in cite37†`COMMAND_REGISTRY`†github.com as a slash command. In Socket Mode, Slack routes the command event through the WebSocket regardless of the manifest's `url` field.
L921: ### Configurationcite74†​ L922:

L980:   * The primary `bot_user_id` (from the first token) is used for backward compatibility with features that expect a single bot identity.

L43: Bundled packages contain the agent, Python, supported dependencies, and prebuilt interfaces. First launch does not build that base runtime. Provider access and optional integrations can still require network access.
L44: 
L45: A `Hermes-Setup` bootstrap installer is different: it downloads a source installation and builds the desktop app. Light is a remote-only build variant, not a bundled local runtime. See cite21†Hermes Desktop .

L49: ### Without Hermes Desktop:cite23†​ L50: 
L51: For a command-line only install without Hermes Desktop, run:
L52: 
L53: #### Linux / macOS / WSL2cite24†​ L54:

L56: 
L57:     curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash
L58: 
L59:     `
L60: 
L61: #### Windows (native)cite25†​ L62:

L66: 
L67:     iex (irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1)
L68: 
L69:     `
L70: 
L71: If you want to install & run Hermes Desktop after a command-line only install, simply run
L72: 
L73:     `
L74: 
L75:     hermes desktop
L76: 
L77:     `
L78: ### Android / Termuxcite26†​ L79: 
L80: Use the cite7†Termux APT package on aarch64 Android devices. Configure its signed repository before running `pkg install hermes-agent`. The desktop/server scripts are not the Termux installation path.
L81: ### What the source installer doescite27†​ L82: The scripts clone the source, bootstrap uv, and delegate dependency preparation to PM. PM provides pinned Python, Node.js, npm, ripgrep, and FFmpeg. The source installation selects the `all` Python extra, not every optional extra. PM also installs the browser and computer-use tools by default: `agent-browser` and its pinned Chromium, and `cua-driver` (the computer-use driver, on macOS, Windows and glibc Linux). If a download fails, the install still completes and prints the command to retry.
L83: The default browser driver (browser-harness, the engine of the Browser Use CLI) is a regular Python dependency, so every install, the Desktop app included, already has it. Other optional tools use their feature-specific installation paths.
L84: To leave the browser tools out, pass `--skip-browser` on POSIX or `-SkipBrowser` on Windows; for the computer-use driver, `--skip-computer-use` / `-SkipComputerUse`. Hermes remembers these choices: later installs and `hermes update` do not add them back. Run `hermes pm install agent-browser` or `hermes pm install cua-driver` to install them and undo the choice.
L85: The scripts create a launcher and prepare the data directory. Interactive runs also invoke setup and gateway configuration. `--non-interactive` on POSIX, or `-NonInteractive` on Windows, skips stages that need input. The optional `--include-desktop` / `-IncludeDesktop` stage builds the desktop from source.
L86: On a terminal the scripts show one status line per step and write the output of git, uv and the builds to `logs/install.log` under the Hermes data directory; a failed step prints its last lines and the log path. CI (`CI` or `GITHUB_ACTIONS` set), redirected output, `--verbose` / `-Verbose` or `HERMES_INSTALL_VERBOSE=1` stream everything instead.
L87: #### Install layoutcite28†​ L88: Method  | Code  | CLI entry point  | Default user data
L89: --- | --- | --- | ---
L90: POSIX source script  | `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/`  | `~/.local/bin/hermes` wrapper  | `~/.hermes/`
L91: Windows source script  | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\hermes-agent\`  | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\bin\`  | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\`
L92: Desktop bundle  | Inside the installed app package  | Packaged launchers; Windows execution aliases  | Platform default Hermes data directory
L93: Docker  | `/opt/hermes/`  | Image entrypoint and `hermes` shim  | Mounted `/opt/data/`
L94: Termux APT  | `$PREFIX/lib/hermes-agent/`  | Symlinks in `$PREFIX/bin/`  | `~/.hermes/`
L95: `HERMES_HOME` selects user data. The POSIX script's `--dir` selects its source checkout independently. Windows provides `-HermesHome` and `-InstallDir`. Running the POSIX script as root does not select an automatic FHS layout: it uses root's home unless you provide an explicit source path.
L96: 
L97: PM's tool store and per-install Python generations have separate lifetimes. See cite29†Package management for their locations. Do not remove the data root to repair an application installation.
L98: ### After Installationcite30†​ L99: 
L100: Reload your shell and start chatting:
L101: 
L102:     `
L103: 
L104:     source ~/.bashrc   # or: source ~/.zshrc
L105: 
L106:     hermes             # Start chatting!
L107: 
L108:     `
L109: To reconfigure individual settings later, use the dedicated commands:
L110: 
L111:     `
L112: 
L113:     hermes model          # Choose your LLM provider and model
L114: 
L115:     hermes tools          # Configure which tools are enabled
L116: 
L117:     hermes gateway setup  # Set up messaging platforms
L118: 
L119:     hermes config set     # Set individual config values
L120: 
L121:     hermes config get     # Inspect individual config values
L122: 
L123:     hermes setup          # Or run the full setup wizard to configure everything at once
L124: 
L125:     `
L126: Fastest path: Nous Portal
L127: 
L128: One subscription covers 300+ models plus the cite31†Tool Gateway (web search, image generation, TTS, cloud browser). Skip the per-tool key juggling:
L129: 
L130:     `
L131: 
L132:     hermes setup --portal
L133: 
L134:     `
L135: 
L136: That logs you in, sets Nous as your provider, and turns on the Tool Gateway in one command.
L137: 
L138: Already running Hermes on another machine?
L139: You don't need to rebuild your setup from scratch. Restore a full backup with `hermes import` (see cite32†Exporting Hermes to another machine ), or bring over a single agent with `hermes profile import` (see cite33†Moving a single profile to another machine ). Note that a profile export excludes credentials by design, so an export alone is not a full backup — cite34†`hermes backup` vs `hermes profile export` explains which to use.
L140: 
L141: * * *
L142: ## Prerequisitescite35†​ L143: 
L144: For the POSIX source script, provide Git, curl, tar, and SHA-256 utilities. Windows can bootstrap its pinned Git for Windows archive when Git is absent. The script always downloads its verified uv pin; a uv already on your PATH is never used.
L145: Current first-party installations run on Python 3.14. The broader `>=3.11,<3.15` range in `pyproject.toml` lets older Python installations run the updater before PM switches them to 3.14; it does not promise current runtime support on 3.11–3.13. PM selects the managed tool versions from `pm/lock.json`; it does not adopt arbitrary system Node versions as the installed runtime.
L146: Source builds can require a native compiler and platform development libraries. Building Electron from source adds Node native-module requirements. These build prerequisites do not apply to installing a complete desktop package. Linux Chromium also requires system libraries supplied by the distribution.

20: class MessageDeduplicator:
21:     """TTL-based message deduplication cache (``if dedup.is_duplicate(msg_id): return``)."""
22: 
23:     def __init__(self, max_size: int = 2000, ttl_seconds: float = 300):
24:         self._seen: dict[str, float] = {}
25:         self._max_size = max_size
26:         self._ttl = ttl_seconds
27: 
28:     def is_duplicate(self, msg_id: str) -> bool:
29:         """Return True if *msg_id* was already seen within the TTL window."""
30:         if not msg_id:
31:             return False
32:         now = time.time()
33:         if msg_id in self._seen:
34:             if now - self._seen[msg_id] < self._ttl:
35:                 return True
36:             del self._seen[msg_id]  # expired: treat as new
37:         self._seen[msg_id] = now
38:         if len(self._seen) > self._max_size:
39:             cutoff = now - self._ttl
40:             self._seen = {k: v for k, v in self._seen.items() if v > cutoff}
41:             if len(self._seen) > self._max_size:
42:                 # All entries still fresh: keep the newest so max_size holds under load.
43:                 self._seen = dict(sorted(self._seen.items(), key=lambda item: item[1])[-self._max_size:])
44:         return False
45: 
46:     def contains(self, msg_id: str) -> bool:
47:         """Return whether *msg_id* is live in the cache without inserting it."""
48:         seen_at = self._seen.get(msg_id) if msg_id else None
49:         if seen_at is None:
50:             return False
51:         if time.time() - seen_at < self._ttl:
52:             return True
53:         del self._seen[msg_id]
54:         return False
55: 
56:     def discard(self, msg_id: str) -> None:
57:         """Release a claimed message ID after cancelled/failed handoff."""
58:         self._seen.pop(msg_id, None)
59: 
60:     def clear(self):
61:         self._seen.clear()
62: 
63:     def absorb(self, other: "MessageDeduplicator") -> None:
64:         """Adopt *other*'s still-live IDs (at their original seen times) into this cache."""
65:         cutoff = time.time() - self._ttl
66:         self._seen.update({k: v for k, v in other._seen.items() if v > cutoff and k not in self._seen})

1: """Durable delivery-obligation ledger for gateway final responses (rows in the shared ``state.db``;
2: WAL, owner pid + process-start liveness, bounded retention) so a crash between finalize and
3: platform ACK cannot lose a response silently. Checkpoints: record_obligation() 'pending' before
4: any send | mark_attempting() 'attempting' right before the await | mark_delivered() 'delivered'
5: only on SendResult.success | mark_failed() 'failed' on a definitive rejection. Crash semantics
6: (never silently resend an ambiguous send): pending = never started, redeliver plainly; attempting
7: = crashed mid-await, platform MAY have it, redeliver WITH a visible recovered marker; failed =
8: rejected once, restart is a retry boundary, also marked; delivered = prune. Attempts are capped
9: and stale rows expire, both -> 'abandoned' (kept briefly, then pruned). Everything is
10: best-effort: ledger failures must never block a send; callers wrap every call in try/except.
11: """
12: 
13: from __future__ import annotations
14: 
15: import hashlib
16: import logging
17: import os
18: import re
19: import sqlite3
20: import threading
21: import time
22: from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional
23: 
24: from gateway.dead_targets import classify_dead_error
25: from hermes_cli.sqlite_util import add_column_if_missing
26: from hermes_constants import get_process_hermes_home
27: 
28: logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
29: _DB_LOCK = threading.Lock()
30: 
31: # Redelivery policy knobs (deliberately not config — the ledger is gated by
32: # ``gateway.delivery_ledger`` and these only matter in the rare recovery path).
33: MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3
34: STALE_AFTER_SECONDS = 24 * 60 * 60
35: _RETENTION_SECONDS = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60
36: _MAX_ROWS = 500
37: 
38: # Visible prefixes for redeliveries that might duplicate an already-received message (crash mid-send /
39: # post-rejection retry) — honest at-least-once. Runtime recovery uses a distinct marker: no restart
40: # occurred, but a network rejection's acknowledgement can still have been lost independently.
41: RECOVERED_MARKER = "♻️ Recovered reply — the gateway restarted during delivery, so this may be a duplicate:\n\n"
42: RECONNECTED_MARKER = ("♻️ Recovered reply — the messaging platform reconnected after the original "
43:                       "delivery failed, so this may be a duplicate:\n\n")
44: # A reply refused by flood control may have gone out as several requests (the adapter chunks long replies,
45: # and MarkdownV2 escaping alone can push a reply that fits one message into two), and the platform may have
46: # accepted the first chunk(s) before refusing the rest; the send result does not say which landed. The raw
47: # length of the stored text says nothing about that, so every flood redelivery carries a marker, and neither
48: # of the markers above tells the truth here (no restart, no reconnect): the rate limit gets its own.
49: FLOOD_MARKER = ("♻️ Recovered reply — the messaging platform's rate limit refused the original, so part of "
50:                 "it may already have arrived above:\n\n")
51: 
52: # Errors whose send contract proves the platform never saw the request: retried as soon as the adapter
53: # is back, no backoff. Every other rejection is retried too (#91653: a 5xx or a transient parse error
54: # used to strand the reply in ``failed`` until the next restart), but only after a backoff that grows
55: # with the attempts already spent, so a platform-side outage is not hammered by the redelivery timer.
56: # A whole-chat death (blocked bot, deleted group, deactivated user) is never retried: the target is gone.
57: _RUNTIME_RETRYABLE_ERRORS = frozenset({"send_path_degraded"})
58: # One tier per in-process retry; the last budgeted attempt is left to the boot sweep (retry_not_before).
59: _RETRY_BACKOFF_SECONDS = (30.0, 120.0)
60: assert len(_RETRY_BACKOFF_SECONDS) == MAX_ATTEMPTS - 1
61: 
62: # A final send the platform refused with flood control is the other transient case: a 429 means the
63: # refused request was never accepted, and the platform said how long to wait. Adapters fail such sends
64: # closed as ``flood_control:<seconds>`` on purpose (#91969) so that this ledger owns the wait instead of
65: # the send coroutine sleeping through it. Before this the row simply sat in ``failed`` until the next
66: # restart's sweep, which then redelivered it hours late under the "gateway restarted during delivery"
67: # marker.
68: FLOOD_ERROR_PREFIX = "flood_control:"
69: FLOOD_RETRY_DEFAULT_SECONDS = 60.0
70: FLOOD_RETRY_CAP_SECONDS = 15 * 60.0
71: FLOOD_RETRY_SLACK_SECONDS = 2.0
72: 
73: # The canonical prefix above is what the adapters produce for a flood they decide not to sleep. It is
74: # not the only shape that reaches this ledger. PTB raises ``RetryAfter``, whose own text reads
75: # "Flood control exceeded. Retry in 185 seconds", and that text is what lands in ``last_error``
76: # whenever a send fails on a path that has not been normalized, or was written by an older build
77: # before it was. Such a row has to be recognised too: unrecognised, it is treated as an ordinary
78: # failure, so no redelivery timer is armed for it and a boot sweep claims it immediately instead of
79: # adopting it until its deadline, spending the one attempt inside the penalty that caused it.
80: # Matching requires the "flood control" wording as well as the delay, so an unrelated error that
81: # merely suggests retrying is never mistaken for a flood.
82: _RAW_FLOOD_RE = re.compile(r"flood control exceeded.*?retry in\s+(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)", re.IGNORECASE)
83: 
84: 
85: def _raw_flood_wait(text: str) -> Optional[float]:
86:     """Seconds asked for by a flood error still carrying the platform's own wording, else ``None``."""
87:     match = _RAW_FLOOD_RE.search(text or "")
88:     if not match:
89:         return None
90:     try:
91:         return float(match.group(1))
92:     except (TypeError, ValueError):
93:         return None
94: 
95: 
96: def is_reconnect_only(error: Any) -> bool:
97:     """True for a row that only an adapter reconnect may retry (no timer, no backoff)."""
98:     return str(error or "").strip().lower() in _RUNTIME_RETRYABLE_ERRORS

22: 
23:     def __init__(self, max_size: int = 2000, ttl_seconds: float = 300):
24:         self._seen: dict[str, float] = {}
25:         self._max_size = max_size
26:         self._ttl = ttl_seconds
27: 
28:     def is_duplicate(self, msg_id: str) -> bool:
29:         """Return True if *msg_id* was already seen within the TTL window."""
30:         if not msg_id:
31:             return False
32:         now = time.time()
33:         if msg_id in self._seen:
34:             if now - self._seen[msg_id] < self._ttl:
35:                 return True
36:             del self._seen[msg_id]  # expired: treat as new
37:         self._seen[msg_id] = now
38:         if len(self._seen) > self._max_size:
39:             cutoff = now - self._ttl
40:             self._seen = {k: v for k, v in self._seen.items() if v > cutoff}
41:             if len(self._seen) > self._max_size:
42:                 # All entries still fresh: keep the newest so max_size holds under load.
43:                 self._seen = dict(sorted(self._seen.items(), key=lambda item: item[1])[-self._max_size:])
44:         return False
45: 
46:     def contains(self, msg_id: str) -> bool:
47:         """Return whether *msg_id* is live in the cache without inserting it."""
48:         seen_at = self._seen.get(msg_id) if msg_id else None
49:         if seen_at is None:
50:             return False
51:         if time.time() - seen_at < self._ttl:
52:             return True
53:         del self._seen[msg_id]
54:         return False

56:     def discard(self, msg_id: str) -> None:
57:         """Release a claimed message ID after cancelled/failed handoff."""
58:         self._seen.pop(msg_id, None)

64:         """Adopt *other*'s still-live IDs (at their original seen times) into this cache."""
65:         cutoff = time.time() - self._ttl
66:         self._seen.update({k: v for k, v in other._seen.items() if v > cutoff and k not in self._seen})

1: """Durable delivery-obligation ledger for gateway final responses (rows in the shared ``state.db``;
2: WAL, owner pid + process-start liveness, bounded retention) so a crash between finalize and
3: platform ACK cannot lose a response silently. Checkpoints: record_obligation() 'pending' before
4: any send | mark_attempting() 'attempting' right before the await | mark_delivered() 'delivered'
5: only on SendResult.success | mark_failed() 'failed' on a definitive rejection. Crash semantics
6: (never silently resend an ambiguous send): pending = never started, redeliver plainly; attempting
7: = crashed mid-await, platform MAY have it, redeliver WITH a visible recovered marker; failed =
8: rejected once, restart is a retry boundary, also marked; delivered = prune. Attempts are capped
9: and stale rows expire, both -> 'abandoned' (kept briefly, then pruned). Everything is
10: best-effort: ledger failures must never block a send; callers wrap every call in try/except.
11: """

47: # length of the stored text says nothing about that, so every flood redelivery carries a marker, and neither
48: # of the markers above tells the truth here (no restart, no reconnect): the rate limit gets its own.
49: FLOOD_MARKER = ("♻️ Recovered reply — the messaging platform's rate limit refused the original, so part of "

21:     """TTL-based message deduplication cache (``if dedup.is_duplicate(msg_id): return``)."""
22: 
23:     def __init__(self, max_size: int = 2000, ttl_seconds: float = 300):
24:         self._seen: dict[str, float] = {}
25:         self._max_size = max_size
26:         self._ttl = ttl_seconds
27: 
28:     def is_duplicate(self, msg_id: str) -> bool:
29:         """Return True if *msg_id* was already seen within the TTL window."""
30:         if not msg_id:
31:             return False
32:         now = time.time()
33:         if msg_id in self._seen:
34:             if now - self._seen[msg_id] < self._ttl:
35:                 return True
36:             del self._seen[msg_id]  # expired: treat as new
37:         self._seen[msg_id] = now
38:         if len(self._seen) > self._max_size:
39:             cutoff = now - self._ttl
40:             self._seen = {k: v for k, v in self._seen.items() if v > cutoff}
41:             if len(self._seen) > self._max_size:
42:                 # All entries still fresh: keep the newest so max_size holds under load.
43:                 self._seen = dict(sorted(self._seen.items(), key=lambda item: item[1])[-self._max_size:])
44:         return False
45: 
46:     def contains(self, msg_id: str) -> bool:
47:         """Return whether *msg_id* is live in the cache without inserting it."""
48:         seen_at = self._seen.get(msg_id) if msg_id else None
49:         if seen_at is None:
50:             return False
51:         if time.time() - seen_at < self._ttl:
52:             return True
53:         del self._seen[msg_id]
54:         return False
55: 
56:     def discard(self, msg_id: str) -> None:
57:         """Release a claimed message ID after cancelled/failed handoff."""
58:         self._seen.pop(msg_id, None)

61:         self._seen.clear()

63:     def absorb(self, other: "MessageDeduplicator") -> None:
64:         """Adopt *other*'s still-live IDs (at their original seen times) into this cache."""
65:         cutoff = time.time() - self._ttl
66:         self._seen.update({k: v for k, v in other._seen.items() if v > cutoff and k not in self._seen})

1: """Durable delivery-obligation ledger for gateway final responses (rows in the shared ``state.db``;
2: WAL, owner pid + process-start liveness, bounded retention) so a crash between finalize and
3: platform ACK cannot lose a response silently. Checkpoints: record_obligation() 'pending' before
4: any send | mark_attempting() 'attempting' right before the await | mark_delivered() 'delivered'
5: only on SendResult.success | mark_failed() 'failed' on a definitive rejection. Crash semantics
6: (never silently resend an ambiguous send): pending = never started, redeliver plainly; attempting
7: = crashed mid-await, platform MAY have it, redeliver WITH a visible recovered marker; failed =
8: rejected once, restart is a retry boundary, also marked; delivered = prune. Attempts are capped
9: and stale rows expire, both -> 'abandoned' (kept briefly, then pruned). Everything is
10: best-effort: ledger failures must never block a send; callers wrap every call in try/except.
11: """
12:

14:

16: import logging
17: import os

19: import sqlite3

21: import time

35: _RETENTION_SECONDS = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60
36: _MAX_ROWS = 500

38: # Visible prefixes for redeliveries that might duplicate an already-received message (crash mid-send /
39: # post-rejection retry) — honest at-least-once. Runtime recovery uses a distinct marker: no restart
40: # occurred, but a network rejection's acknowledgement can still have been lost independently.
41: RECOVERED_MARKER = "♻️ Recovered reply — the gateway restarted during delivery, so this may be a duplicate:\n\n"
42: RECONNECTED_MARKER = ("♻️ Recovered reply — the messaging platform reconnected after the original "
43:                       "delivery failed, so this may be a duplicate:\n\n")
44: # A reply refused by flood control may have gone out as several requests (the adapter chunks long replies,
45: # and MarkdownV2 escaping alone can push a reply that fits one message into two), and the platform may have
46: # accepted the first chunk(s) before refusing the rest; the send result does not say which landed. The raw
47: # length of the stored text says nothing about that, so every flood redelivery carries a marker, and neither
48: # of the markers above tells the truth here (no restart, no reconnect): the rate limit gets its own.
49: FLOOD_MARKER = ("♻️ Recovered reply — the messaging platform's rate limit refused the original, so part of "
50:                 "it may already have arrived above:\n\n")
51: 
52: # Errors whose send contract proves the platform never saw the request: retried as soon as the adapter
53: # is back, no backoff. Every other rejection is retried too (#91653: a 5xx or a transient parse error
54: # used to strand the reply in ``failed`` until the next restart), but only after a backoff that grows
55: # with the attempts already spent, so a platform-side outage is not hammered by the redelivery timer.
56: # A whole-chat death (blocked bot, deleted group, deactivated user) is never retried: the target is gone.
57: _RUNTIME_RETRYABLE_ERRORS = frozenset({"send_path_degraded"})
58: # One tier per in-process retry; the last budgeted attempt is left to the boot sweep (retry_not_before).
59: _RETRY_BACKOFF_SECONDS = (30.0, 120.0)
60: assert len(_RETRY_BACKOFF_SECONDS) == MAX_ATTEMPTS - 1
61: 
62: # A final send the platform refused with flood control is the other transient case: a 429 means the
63: # refused request was never accepted, and the platform said how long to wait. Adapters fail such sends
64: # closed as ``flood_control:<seconds>`` on purpose (#91969) so that this ledger owns the wait instead of
65: # the send coroutine sleeping through it. Before this the row simply sat in ``failed`` until the next
66: # restart's sweep, which then redelivered it hours late under the "gateway restarted during delivery"
67: # marker.
68: FLOOD_ERROR_PREFIX = "flood_control:"
69: FLOOD_RETRY_DEFAULT_SECONDS = 60.0
70: FLOOD_RETRY_CAP_SECONDS = 15 * 60.0
71: FLOOD_RETRY_SLACK_SECONDS = 2.0

73: # The canonical prefix above is what the adapters produce for a flood they decide not to sleep. It is

1: """Durable delivery-obligation ledger for gateway final responses (rows in the shared ``state.db``;
2: WAL, owner pid + process-start liveness, bounded retention) so a crash between finalize and
3: platform ACK cannot lose a response silently. Checkpoints: record_obligation() 'pending' before

6: (never silently resend an ambiguous send): pending = never started, redeliver plainly; attempting
7: = crashed mid-await, platform MAY have it, redeliver WITH a visible recovered marker; failed =
8: rejected once, restart is a retry boundary, also marked; delivered = prune. Attempts are capped
9: and stale rows expire, both -> 'abandoned' (kept briefly, then pruned). Everything is
10: best-effort: ledger failures must never block a send; callers wrap every call in try/except.

Yes. Background/recovery and hosted acceptance remain **runtime unverified**, with several narrower source-backed limitations worth adding to the research report.

**Version baseline**

The latest published stable release currently resolves to **Hermes v0.21.5, tag `v2026.9.24`, commit `f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f`**. Main resolved separately to `4ed093cb6be8a2fadb39e770898f6989fc67201d` dated October 2. Treat live website docs as moving documentation; yyot has not selected or exercised a baseline. [Release](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/releases/tag/v2026.9.24)

**Supported primitives and remaining verification**

| Area | What research establishes | What yyot still must prove |
|---|---|---|
| Acknowledgement/progress | `/bg` immediately acknowledges and creates a separate context; messaging supports progress/status, clarification and `/stop`. | Prompt ordinary-request acknowledgement, useful brief updates, correct private audience, private human handoff, and effective cancellation of the actual browser/delegated work. |
| History/recovery | Gateway persists sessions and marks interrupted turns for recovery. | Preserve original task, owner/audience, history and artifacts across planned restart and hard crash; resume after expired access without losing context. |
| Final reply delivery | Durable `state.db` delivery ledger preserves final responses and redelivers ambiguous sends with duplicate warning. | Correct Slack destination/profile/thread after restart; tolerate duplicate replies honestly; prevent replaying website actions to regenerate a missing reply. |
| Execution bounds | Iteration budgets and inactivity timeouts exist. Delegation default has no wall-clock timeout. | Chosen task/time/cost bounds actually terminate all relevant work. Do not describe an inactivity cap as a total runtime cap. |
| Hosting | Slack Socket Mode needs no public HTTP endpoint. Docker supports mounted persistent data; service supervision is documented. | Hosted reviewer journey, refresh/reboot behavior, durable storage and browser state, appropriate resources, and operation with the laptop absent. |

The first three rows draw on [Messaging Gateway](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/); bounds on [Subagent Delegation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/delegation/) and [environment variables](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/reference/environment-variables/); hosting on [Slack setup](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/slack/) and [Docker](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/docker/).

**Two concrete source findings**

1. **Reply durability is not exactly-once browser execution.** At the pinned release, `gateway/delivery_ledger.py:1–10` explicitly concerns *final responses*, is best effort, and labels ambiguous resends; its limits are three attempts and 24-hour freshness. This is useful upstream functionality, but no proof that a purchase/upload/publication accepted before a crash will not repeat. Interactive recovery also injects instructions to report restoration and avoid reexecuting old calls, rather than implementing an external-action transaction. [Delivery ledger source](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/gateway/delivery_ledger.py#L1), [recovery-note source](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/gateway/run.py#L1034)

2. **Slack deduplication is memory-based.** The adapter suppresses repeated `team_id:event_ts` keys, with a one-hour default TTL. `MessageDeduplicator` stores a Python dict and can transfer entries when replacing an adapter in the same process. That mechanism does not itself persist across a whole gateway restart. Avoid claiming that every replay is unsafe, since a complete runtime test may find other protection; retain duplicate-event-after-restart as a specific open check. [Slack dedupe configuration](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py#L865), [ingress dedupe](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py#L4368), [cache implementation](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/gateway/platforms/helpers.py#L20)

**Hosting nuance**

Cron is not automatically equivalent to durable conversational browser work. The docs describe persisted jobs and restart-safe external workers **when systemd user scopes are available**. Without those scopes, cron may degrade to workers killed by gateway restart; `cron.require_restart_safe_scope: true` can refuse that configuration. Container-wide/host restart remains a different failure boundary. Use this only if cron is the selected execution path, rather than adding it unnecessarily. [Cron restart-safe workers](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/cron/#restart-safe-workers-under-systemd)

Docker docs recommend at least **2 GB memory with browser tools** and persist data via `/opt/data`. Mount/configuration presence must be followed by restart verification. Backup/export is also distinct from runtime persistence: browser profiles are excluded from current documented `hermes backup`, so a backup restore must not be assumed to preserve signed-in browser sessions. [Docker resources](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/docker/#resource-limits), [backup reference](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/reference/cli-commands/)

**Exact remaining V5 experiment**

1. Start an owner-private task, measure acknowledgement/progress, pause for private login/input, and resume that same task.
2. Execute fake consequential submissions with a server-side counter; stop before action, after acceptance before result persistence, and before Slack delivery.
3. Restart and reconcile actual server state; require one intended submission, correct owner/audience, and truthful uncertainty instead of blind retry.
4. Replay the same Slack event before and after process restart; verify no duplicated submission or authority.
5. Cancel foreground and delegated/background variants; check the counter and processes for later side effects, then prove configured execution bounds and durable artifacts with the laptop absent.

Existing upstream tests worth inspecting/running against the selected version:

- `tests/gateway/test_active_turn_recovery.py`
- `tests/gateway/test_restart_resume_pending.py`
- `tests/gateway/test_delivery_ledger.py`
- `tests/gateway/test_slack_dedup_ttl.py`
- `tests/gateway/test_stop_ends_background_delegations.py`

These are upstream evidence leads, **not yyot test passes**. No runtime, deployment, repository mutation, or external action was performed.

3. Restart and reconcile actual server state; require one intended submission, correct owner/audience, and truthful uncertainty instead of blind retry.
4. Replay the same Slack event before and after process restart; verify no duplicated submission or authority.
5. Cancel foreground and delegated/background variants; check the counter and processes for later side effects, then prove configured execution bounds and durable artifacts with the laptop absent.

- `tests/gateway/test_delivery_ledger.py`
- `tests/gateway/test_slack_dedup_ttl.py`
