L43: ## cite7†Control groups L44: 
L45: Control Groups are another key component of Linux containers. They implement resource accounting and limiting. They provide many useful metrics, but they also help ensure that each container gets its fair share of memory, CPU, disk I/O; and, more importantly, that a single container cannot bring the system down by exhausting one of those resources.
L46: So while they do not play a role in preventing one container from accessing or affecting the data and processes of another container, they are essential to fend off some denial-of-service attacks. They are particularly important on multi-tenant platforms, like public and private PaaS, to guarantee a consistent uptime (and performance) even when some applications start to misbehave.
L47: 
L48: Control Groups have been around for a while as well: the code was started in 2006, and initially merged in kernel 2.6.24.
L49: ## cite8†Docker daemon attack surface L50: 
L51: Running containers (and applications) with Docker implies running the Docker daemon. This daemon requires `root` privileges unless you opt-in to cite17†Rootless mode , and you should therefore be aware of some important details.
L52: First of all, only trusted users should be allowed to control your Docker daemon. This is a direct consequence of some powerful Docker features. Specifically, Docker allows you to share a directory between the Docker host and a guest container; and it allows you to do so without limiting the access rights of the container. This means that you can start a container where the `/host` directory is the `/` directory on your host; and the container can alter your host filesystem without any restriction.
L53: This is similar to how virtualization systems allow filesystem resource sharing. Nothing prevents you from sharing your root filesystem (or even your root block device) with a virtual machine.
L54: This has a strong security implication: for example, if you instrument Docker from a web server to provision containers through an API, you should be even more careful than usual with parameter checking, to make sure that a malicious user cannot pass crafted parameters causing Docker to create arbitrary containers.
L55: For this reason, the REST API endpoint (used by the Docker CLI to communicate with the Docker daemon) changed in Docker 0.5.2, and now uses a Unix socket instead of a TCP socket bound on 127.0.0.1 (the latter being prone to cross-site request forgery attacks if you happen to run Docker directly on your local machine, outside of a VM). You can then use traditional Unix permission checks to limit access to the control socket.
L56: You can also expose the REST API over HTTP if you explicitly decide to do so. However, if you do that, be aware of the above mentioned security implications. Note that even if you have a firewall to limit accesses to the REST API endpoint from other hosts in the network, the endpoint can be still accessible from containers, and it can easily result in the privilege escalation. Therefore it is mandatory to secure API endpoints with cite18†HTTPS and certificates .
L57: Exposing the daemon API over HTTP without TLS is not permitted, and such a configuration causes the daemon to fail early on startup, see cite19†Unauthenticated TCP connections . It is also recommended to ensure that it is reachable only from a trusted network or VPN.
L58: You can also use `DOCKER_HOST=ssh://USER@HOST` or `ssh -L /path/to/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` instead if you prefer SSH over TLS.
L59: The daemon is also potentially vulnerable to other inputs, such as image loading from either disk with `docker load`, or from the network with `docker pull`. As of Docker 1.3.2, images are now extracted in a chrooted subprocess on Linux/Unix platforms, being the first-step in a wider effort toward privilege separation. As of Docker 1.10.0, all images are stored and accessed by the cryptographic checksums of their contents, limiting the possibility of an attacker causing a collision with an existing image.
L60: Finally, if you run Docker on a server, it is recommended to run exclusively Docker on the server, and move all other services within containers controlled by Docker. Of course, it is fine to keep your favorite admin tools (probably at least an SSH server), as well as existing monitoring/supervision processes, such as NRPE and collectd.
L61: ## cite9†Linux kernel capabilities L62: 
L63: By default, Docker starts containers with a restricted set of capabilities. What does that mean?
L64: Capabilities turn the binary "root/non-root" dichotomy into a fine-grained access control system. Processes (like web servers) that just need to bind on a port below 1024 do not need to run as root: they can just be granted the `net_bind_service` capability instead. And there are many other capabilities, for almost all the specific areas where root privileges are usually needed. This means a lot for container security.
L65: Typical servers run several processes as `root`, including the SSH daemon, `cron` daemon, logging daemons, kernel modules, network configuration tools, and more. A container is different, because almost all of those tasks are handled by the infrastructure around the container:
L66:   * SSH access are typically managed by a single server running on the Docker host
L67:   * `cron`, when necessary, should run as a user process, dedicated and tailored for the app that needs its scheduling service, rather than as a platform-wide facility
L68:   * Log management is also typically handed to Docker, or to third-party services like Loggly or Splunk
L69:   * Hardware management is irrelevant, meaning that you never need to run `udevd` or equivalent daemons within containers
L70:   * Network management happens outside of the containers, enforcing separation of concerns as much as possible, meaning that a container should never need to perform `ifconfig`, `route`, or ip commands (except when a container is specifically engineered to behave like a router or firewall, of course)
L71: This means that in most cases, containers do not need "real" root privileges at all* And therefore, containers can run with a reduced capability set; meaning that "root" within a container has much less privileges than the real "root". For instance, it is possible to:
L72:   * Deny all "mount" operations
L73:   * Deny access to raw sockets (to prevent packet spoofing)
L74:   * Deny access to some filesystem operations, like creating new device nodes, changing the owner of files, or altering attributes (including the immutable flag)
L75:   * Deny module loading
L76: 
L77: This means that even if an intruder manages to escalate to root within a container, it is much harder to do serious damage, or to escalate to the host.
L78: This doesn't affect regular web apps, but reduces the vectors of attack by malicious users considerably. By default Docker drops all capabilities except cite20†those needed†github.com , an allowlist instead of a denylist approach. You can see a full list of available capabilities in cite21†Linux manpages†man7.org .
L80: Docker supports the addition and removal of capabilities, allowing use of a non-default profile. This may make Docker more secure through capability removal, or less secure through the addition of capabilities. The best practice for users would be to remove all capabilities except those explicitly required for their processes.
L81: ## cite10†Docker Content Trust signature verification L82: 
L83: Docker Engine can be configured to only run signed images. The Docker Content Trust signature verification feature is built directly into the `dockerd` binary.
L84: This is configured in the Dockerd configuration file.
L85: 
L86: To enable this feature, trustpinning can be configured in `daemon.json`, whereby only repositories signed with a user-specified root key can be pulled and run.
L96:   * If your distribution comes with security model templates for Docker containers, you can use them out of the box. For instance, we ship a template that works with AppArmor and Red Hat comes with SELinux policies for Docker. #     (chown, profile reconcile, dashboard toggle) and sets up the
#     supervision tree before any service starts. Bypassing it skips
#     all of that setup and the gateway will not work correctly.
#   - The gateway's API server is off unless you uncomment API_SERVER_KEY
#     and API_SERVER_HOST. See docs/user-guide/api-server.md before doing
#     this on an internet-facing host.
#
services:
  gateway:
    build: .
    image: hermes-agent
    container_name: hermes
    restart: unless-stopped
    network_mode: host
    volumes:
      - ~/.hermes:/opt/data
    environment:
      - HERMES_UID=${HERMES_UID:-10000}
      - HERMES_GID=${HERMES_GID:-10000}
      # To expose the OpenAI-compatible API server beyond localhost,
      # uncomment BOTH lines (API_SERVER_KEY is mandatory for auth):
      # - API_SERVER_HOST=0.0.0.0
      # - API_SERVER_KEY=${API_SERVER_KEY}
      # Microsoft Teams — uncomment and fill in to enable Teams gateway.
      # Register your bot at https://dev.botframework.com/ to get these values.
      # - TEAMS_CLIENT_ID=${TEAMS_CLIENT_ID}
      # - TEAMS_CLIENT_SECRET=${TEAMS_CLIENT_SECRET}
      # - TEAMS_TENANT_ID=${TEAMS_TENANT_ID}
      # - TEAMS_ALLOWED_USERS=${TEAMS_ALLOWED_USERS}
# 502 / "[session ended]". Pointing at the prebuilt bundle sidesteps the whole
# check. (A separate launcher hardening is tracked independently.)
ENV HERMES_TUI_DIR=/opt/hermes/ui-tui
ENV HERMES_HOME=/opt/data
ENV HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT=/opt/data
ENV HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS=1
# The published image seals /opt/hermes (root-owned, read-only) so a runtime
# lazy install can't mutate the agent's own venv and brick it. But opt-in
- **`openssh-client`** — enables the [SSH terminal backend](./configuration.md#ssh-backend) from inside the container. The SSH backend shells out to the system `ssh` binary; without this, it failed silently in containerized installs.
- The WhatsApp bridge (`scripts/whatsapp-bridge/`)
- **[`s6-overlay`](https://github.com/just-containers/s6-overlay) v3** as PID 1 (replaces the older `tini`) — supervises the dashboard and per-profile gateways with auto-restart on crash, reaps zombie subprocesses, and forwards signals.

The image treats `/opt/hermes` as an immutable install tree at runtime. Optional Python extras, Node workspaces, and TUI assets that must be available inside Docker need to be baked during the image build; runtime lazy installs are disabled so supervised gateways and `docker exec hermes …` commands do not try to write dependency artifacts back into the read-only source tree.

The container's `ENTRYPOINT` is a small dispatcher (`docker/entrypoint-dispatch.sh`). When the container owns PID 1 (normal Docker / Podman), it exec's s6-overlay's `/init` and you get the full supervision tree described below. When a platform wraps the image entrypoint under its own PID-1 init (Fly.io Machines, `docker run --init`, some Nomad/Kubernetes setups), `/init` would abort with `s6-overlay-suexec: fatal: can only run as pid 1` — so the dispatcher instead runs the stage2 bootstrap directly and exec's the main wrapper without s6. On that fallback path the requested command still runs, but supervised services (dashboard, per-profile gateways) are unavailable.

On the PID-1 path, `/init`:
1. Runs `/etc/cont-init.d/01-hermes-setup` (= `docker/stage2-hook.sh`) as root: optional UID/GID remap, fixes volume ownership, seeds `.env` / `config.yaml` / `SOUL.md` on first boot, runs non-interactive config-schema migrations unless `HERMES_SKIP_CONFIG_MIGRATION=1`, syncs bundled skills.
2. Runs `/etc/cont-init.d/02-reconcile-profiles` (= `hermes_cli.container_boot`): walks `$HERMES_HOME/profiles/<name>/`, recreates the per-profile gateway s6 service slot under `/run/service/gateway-<profile>/`, and auto-starts only those whose last recorded state was `running` (see [Per-profile gateway supervision](#per-profile-gateway-supervision)).
3. Starts the static `main-hermes` and `dashboard` s6-rc services.
4. Exec's the container's CMD as the main program (`/opt/hermes/docker/main-wrapper.sh`), which routes the arguments the user passed to `docker run`:
   - no args → `hermes` (the default)
   - first arg is an executable on PATH (e.g. `sleep`, `bash`) → exec it directly
   - anything else → `hermes <args>` (subcommand passthrough)
   The container exits when this main program exits, with its exit code.

:::warning Breaking change vs. pre-s6 images
The container ENTRYPOINT is now the `entrypoint-dispatch.sh` dispatcher (which delegates to s6-overlay's `/init` under PID 1), not `/usr/bin/tini`. All five documented `docker run` invocation patterns (no args, `chat -q "…"`, `sleep infinity`, `bash`, `--tui`) behave identically to the tini-based image. If you have a downstream wrapper that depended on tini-specific signal behavior or hard-coded `/usr/bin/tini --` invocation, pin to the previous image tag.
:::

:::warning Privilege model
Do not override the image entrypoint unless you keep `/init` (or, equivalently, the legacy `docker/entrypoint.sh` shim that forwards to the stage2 hook) in the command chain. s6-overlay's `/init` runs as root so it can chown the volume on first boot, then drops to the `hermes` user via `s6-setuidgid` for every supervised service AND for the main program. Starting `hermes gateway run` as root inside the official image is refused by default because it can leave root-owned files in `/opt/data` and break later dashboard or gateway starts. Set `HERMES_ALLOW_ROOT_GATEWAY=1` only when you intentionally accept that risk.
:::

:::warning Overriding `entrypoint:` also removes the zombie reaper

class Colima < Formula
  desc "Container runtimes on MacOS (and Linux) with minimal setup"
  homepage "https://github.com/abiosoft/colima/blob/main/README.md"
  url "https://github.com/abiosoft/colima.git",

  livecheck do
    url :stable
    regex(/^v?(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)$/i)

item.stdout:
Colima provides container runtimes on macOS with minimal setup.

Usage:
  colima [command]

Available Commands:
  completion  Generate completion script
  delete      delete and teardown Colima
  help        Help about any command
  kubernetes  manage Kubernetes cluster
  list        list instances
  model       manage AI models (requires docker runtime and krunkit VM type)
  nerdctl     run nerdctl (requires containerd runtime)
  prune       prune cached downloaded assets
  restart     restart Colima
  ssh         SSH into the VM
  ssh-config  show SSH connection config
  start       start Colima
  status      show the status of Colima
  stop        stop Colima
  template    edit the template for default configurations
  update      update the container runtime
  version     print the version of Colima

Flags:
  -h, --help             help for colima
  -p, --profile string   profile name, for multiple instances (default "default")
  -v, --verbose          enable verbose log
      --version          version for colima
      --very-verbose     enable more verbose log

Use "colima [command] --help" for more information about a command.
Start Colima with the specified container runtime and optional kubernetes.

Colima can also be configured with a YAML file.
Run 'colima template' to set the default configurations or 'colima start --edit' to customize before startup.

Usage:
  colima start [profile] [flags]

Examples:
  colima start
  colima start --edit
  colima start --foreground

L0:   * cite0†Home L1:   * cite1†Documentation L2:   * cite2†Announcements L3:   * cite3†Community L4:   * cite4†31.1K†github.com cite5†Sponsor L5:   *   * cite6†Getting Started L6:   * cite7†Installation L7:   * cite8†Commands L8:   * cite9†Configuration L9:   * cite10†Runtimes L10:   * cite11†Profiles L11:     * cite12†Understanding Profiles L12:     * cite13†Creating Profiles L13:     * cite14†Listing Profiles L14:     * cite15†Starting and Stopping Instances L15:       * cite16†Starting an Instance L16:       * cite17†Stopping an Instance L17:       * cite18†Restarting an Instance L18:     * cite19†Deleting Instances L19:       * cite20†Soft Delete (Preserve Container Data) L20:       * cite21†Complete Teardown L21:     * cite22†Specifying a Profile L22:       * cite23†Profile as Argument L23:       * cite24†Profile as Flag L24:       * cite25†Environment Variable L25:       * cite26†Other Relevant Environment Variables L26:     * cite27†Common Use Cases L27:       * cite28†Different Environments L28:       * cite29†Multiple Container Runtimes L29:       * cite30†Testing Different Architectures L30:       * cite31†Kubernetes Development L31:     * cite32†Docker Context with Profiles L32:   * cite33†AI Workloads L33:   * cite34†FAQ L34: # Profiles
L35: 
L36: A profile in Colima is an independent instance of a virtual machine with its own configuration, runtime, and container data. Profiles allow you to run multiple isolated environments simultaneously, each with different settings tailored to specific use cases.
L37: ## cite12†Understanding Profiles L38: 
L39: Each profile is a completely separate Colima instance with:
L40: 
L41:   * Its own VM resources (CPU, memory, disk)
L42:   * Its own container runtime (Docker, Containerd, or Incus)
L43:   * Its own containers, images, and volumes
L44:   * Its own configuration file at `~/.colima/<profile>/colima.yaml`
L45: 
L46: The default profile is named `default` and is used when no profile is specified.
L47: ## cite13†Creating Profiles L48: 
L49: Create a new profile by specifying a name when starting Colima:
L50: 
L51:     `# Create a profile named "dev"
L52:     colima start dev
L53: 
L54:     # Create a profile with custom resources
L55:     colima start dev --cpus 4 --memory 8
L56: 
L57:     # Create a profile with Kubernetes
L58:     colima start k8s --kubernetes
L59: 
L60:     # Create a profile with containerd runtime
L61:     colima start containerd --runtime containerd
L62:     `
L63: 
L64: Each profile name creates a new, independent instance.
L65: ## cite14†Listing Profiles L66: 
L67: View all profiles and their status:
L68: 
L69:     `colima list
L70:     `
L71: 
L72: Example output:
L73: 
L74:     `PROFILE    STATUS     ARCH       CPUS    MEMORY    DISK     RUNTIME
L75:     default    Running    aarch64    4       8GiB      100GiB   docker
L76:     dev        Running    aarch64    2       4GiB      60GiB    docker
L77:     k8s        Stopped    aarch64    4       8GiB      100GiB   docker
L78:     `
L79: 
L80: ## cite15†Starting and Stopping Instances L81: ### cite16†Starting an Instance L82: 
L83: Start an existing profile:
L84: 
L85:     `# Start the default profile
L86:     colima start
L87: 
L88:     # Start a named profile (profile as argument)
L89:     colima start dev
L90: 
L91:     # Start using the --profile flag
L92:     colima start --profile dev
L93:     `
L94: ### cite17†Stopping an Instance L95: 
L96: Stop a running profile:
L97: 
L98:     `# Stop the default profile
L99:     colima stop
L100: 
L101:     # Stop a named profile (profile as argument)
L102:     colima stop dev
L103: 
L104:     # Stop using the --profile flag
L105:     colima stop --profile dev
L106:     `
L107: 
L108: ### cite18†Restarting an Instance L109: 
L110: Restart a profile:
L111: 
L112:     `# Restart the default profile
L113:     colima restart
L114: 
L115:     # Restart a named profile
L116:     colima restart dev
L117:     `
L118: 
L119: ## cite19†Deleting Instances L120: ### cite20†Soft Delete (Preserve Container Data) L121: 
L122: Delete the VM instance while retaining container data (images, volumes):
L123: 
L124:     `# Delete the default profile
L125:     colima delete
L126: 
L127:     # Delete a named profile
L128:     colima delete dev
L129:     `
L130: 
L131: This removes the VM but preserves container data. When you recreate the profile with the same name, the container data will be restored.
L132: 
L133: See cite35†Data Persistence for more.
L134: ### cite21†Complete Teardown L135: 
L136: Delete the VM instance and all associated data including containers, images, and volumes:
L137: 
L138:     `# Completely remove the default profile
L139:     colima delete --data
L140: 
L141:     # Completely remove a named profile
L142:     colima delete dev --data
L143: 
L144:     # Force delete without confirmation
L145:     colima delete dev --data --force
L146:     `
L147: 
L148: The `--data` flag ensures a complete cleanup, removing:
L149:   * The virtual machine
L150:   * All container images
L151:   * All container volumes
L152:   * All configuration files
L153: 
L154: Use this when you want to start fresh or reclaim disk space.
L155: ## cite22†Specifying a Profile L156: 
L157: There are three ways to specify which profile to use:
L158: 
L159: ### cite23†Profile as Argument L160: 
L161: Commands like `start`, `stop`, `delete`, and `restart` accept the profile name as an argument:
L162: 
L163:     `colima start dev
L164:     colima stop dev
L165:     colima delete dev
L166:     colima restart dev
L167:     `
L168: ### cite24†Profile as Flag L169: 
L170: All commands support the `--profile` (or `-p`) flag:
L171: 
L172:     `colima start --profile dev
L173:     colima stop --profile dev
L174:     colima status --profile dev
L175:     colima ssh --profile dev
L176:     colima list --profile dev
L177:     `
L178: ### cite25†Environment Variable L179: 
L180: Set the `COLIMA_PROFILE` environment variable to avoid specifying the profile with every command:
L181: 
L182:     `# Set for the current session
L183:     export COLIMA_PROFILE=dev
L184: 
L185:     # Now all commands use the "dev" profile
L186:     colima start
L187:     colima status
L188:     colima stop
L189:     `
L190: 
L191: Add to your shell configuration (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`, etc.) for persistence:
L192: 
L193:     `export COLIMA_PROFILE=dev
L194:     `
L195: The environment variable is especially useful when you primarily work with a single non-default profile.
L196: 
L197: Priority: `--profile` flag > command argument > `COLIMA_PROFILE` environment variable > default profile.
L198: ### cite26†Other Relevant Environment Variables L199: 
L200: Variable  | Description
L201: --- | ---
L202: `COLIMA_HOME`  | Base directory for all profiles (default: `~/.colima`)
L203: `COLIMA_PROFILE`  | Active profile name (default: `default`)
L204: `DOCKER_CONFIG`  | Path to Docker client configuration directory (default: `~/.docker`)
L205: 
L206: ## cite27†Common Use Cases L207: ### cite28†Different Environments L208: 
L209:     `# Development: more resources, SSH agent forwarding
L210:     colima start dev --cpus 4 --memory 8 --ssh-agent
L211: 
L212:     # CI: minimal resources
L213:     colima start ci --cpus 2 --memory 2
L214:     `
L215: 
L216: ### cite29†Multiple Container Runtimes L217: 
L218:     `# Docker runtime (default)
L219:     colima start docker
L220: 
L221:     # Containerd runtime
L222:     colima start containerd --runtime containerd
L223: 
L224:     # Incus runtime
L225:     colima start incus --runtime incus
L226:     `
L227: ### cite30†Testing Different Architectures L228: 
L229:     `# Native architecture
L230:     colima start native
L231: 
L232:     # x86_64 on Apple Silicon
L233:     colima start x86 --arch x86_64
L234:     `
L235: 
L236: ### cite31†Kubernetes Development L237: 
L238:     `# Kubernetes cluster
L239:     colima start k8s --kubernetes --cpus 4 --memory 8
L240: 
L241:     # Multiple Kubernetes versions
L242:     colima start k8s-128 --kubernetes --kubernetes-version v1.28.3+k3s1
L243:     colima start k8s-127 --kubernetes --kubernetes-version v1.27.7+k3s1
L244:     `
L245: ## cite32†Docker Context with Profiles L246: 
L247: Each profile creates its own Docker context. Switch between them:
L248: 
L249:     `# List Docker contexts
L250:     docker context ls
L251: 
L252:     # Use a specific profile's context
L253:     docker context use colima-dev
L254: 
L255:     # Use the default profile's context
L256:     docker context use colima
L257:     `
L258:

*** Add File: /Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/verification/RUNTIME_SETUP.md
+# Local container runtime setup
+
+Status: **Colima installed; VM creation blocked by insufficient free disk.** No Colima VM/profile or Hermes container was created or started. No login credentials were copied, no autostart service was registered, and no cleanup was performed.
+
+## Completed
+
+Host: Apple Silicon macOS 26.5.2. Installed the official Homebrew formula and its dependency:
+
+| Package | Installed version | Location |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Colima | 0.10.1, commit `ed905203afdbc6fd4eae6cc301918099ff31e86e` | `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/colima/0.10.1` |
+| Lima | 2.0.3 | `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/lima/2.0.3` |
+
+Command executed:
+
+```bash
+HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1 \
+HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALL_UPGRADE=1 \
+HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALL_CLEANUP=1 \
+HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALLED_DEPENDENTS_CHECK=1 \
+  /opt/homebrew/bin/brew install colima
+```
+
+Homebrew installed the `arm64_tahoe` bottles successfully. The package-manager flags/environment settings avoided unrelated upgrades and cleanup. `colima version` and `limactl --version` confirmed the versions above. `colima list --json` returned no instances. `docker context ls` still showed the personal `desktop-linux` context selected and its existing missing Docker Desktop socket; no active-context change occurred.
+
+Before choosing commands, inspected `brew install --help`, `brew info --help`, `colima --help`, `colima start --help`, `colima template --help`, `colima list --help`, and Docker help. No `brew services` command was run.
+
+## Disk blocker
+
+After installation, `df -h /Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot` reported the data volume at **99% capacity**, with **3.3 GiB available**. A separate `os.statvfs` check measured **3,556,270,080 available bytes (3.31 GiB)**.
+
+The planned guest has a 20 GiB container-data disk **and a separate 20 GiB root disk**, plus downloaded images and later build storage. These virtual disks are sparse, but the current physical headroom is too small to proceed safely. The local preflight required at least 50 GiB free for this plan; that is a conservative lab allocation check, not a published Colima minimum. VM start was not attempted, and there was no cleanup or fallback to broader host mounts.
+
+## Proposed start command — not executed
+
+Once the storage blocker is resolved, recheck free space before starting. Use a dedicated `clanker-lab` profile and separate Colima/Docker client state:
+
+```bash
+env -i \
+  HOME="$HOME" \
+  PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH" \
+  COLIMA_HOME=/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/colima \
+  DOCKER_CONFIG=/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/docker-client \
+  /opt/homebrew/bin/colima start clanker-lab \
+    --template=false \
+    --runtime docker \
+    --vm-type vz \
+    --arch aarch64 \
+    --cpus 2 \
+    --memory 4 \
+    --disk 20 \
+    --root-disk 20 \
+    --mount none \
+    --activate=false \
+    --ssh-agent=false \
+    --ssh-config=false \
+    --port-forwarder none \
+    --binfmt=false
+```
+
+The installed CLI explicitly documents `--mount none` as disabling directory mounts. An empty `mounts: []` configuration is **not** the same instruction: the pinned default describes a writable host-home mount. `--activate=false` prevents automatic Docker context selection. `--ssh-config=false` prevents modification of the personal SSH config, and SSH agent forwarding stays disabled. `--template=false` avoids inheriting personal template settings. Native `vz` avoids installing QEMU or enabling Rosetta. Guest provisioning will download the official Colima core image when first started; that download has not occurred.
+
+After a successful start, inspect the created guest configuration for absent host mounts and verify the Docker server only through the dedicated client state and explicit `colima-clanker-lab` context. Do not fall back to the personal/default daemon if that context fails. Do not mount the project, host home, Docker control socket, or Slack/OAuth credentials. This stage ends when the empty Docker runtime is verified; Hermes builds and two-owner boundary experiments are separate work.
+
+## Sources
+
+- [Official Colima installation instructions](https://github.com/abiosoft/colima): Homebrew installation and Docker client integration.
+- [Colima profiles](https://colima.run/docs/profiles/): per-profile VMs, `COLIMA_HOME`, `DOCKER_CONFIG`, and Docker context naming.
+- [Pinned Colima 0.10.1 default configuration](https://github.com/abiosoft/colima/blob/v0.10.1/embedded/defaults/colima.yaml): default host mounts, auto activation, separate root disk, SSH behavior, and official guest-image source.
+- Installed `colima start --help`: exact flags and behavior used in the unexecuted command above.
+
+This prepares a Linux VM/container runtime boundary. Distinct Hermes `HERMES_HOME` directories alone remain configuration separation. The eventual two-owner test must place the complete runtime, browser/MCP processes, credentials, workspace, memory, sessions, and artifacts inside separate owner containers and prove cross-owner access is denied.
*** End Patch"));

Usage:
  colima start [profile] [flags]

  colima start
  colima start --edit
  colima start --foreground
  colima start --runtime containerd

  colima start --cpu 4 --memory 8 --disk 100
  colima start --arch aarch64

  colima start --kubernetes --k3s-arg='"--disable=coredns,servicelb,traefik,local-storage,metrics-server"'

Flags:
      --activate                    set as active Docker/Kubernetes/Incus context on startup (default true)
  -a, --arch string                 architecture (aarch64, x86_64) (default "aarch64")
      --binfmt                      use binfmt for foreign architecture emulation (no-op if Rosetta is enabled) (default true)
      --cpu-type string             the CPU type, options can be checked with 'qemu-system-aarch64 -cpu help'
  -c, --cpus int                    number of CPUs (default 2)
  -d, --disk int                    disk size in GiB (default 100)
  -i, --disk-image string           file path to a custom disk image
  -n, --dns ipSlice                 DNS resolvers for the VM (default [])
      --dns-host strings            custom DNS names to provide to resolver
  -e, --edit                        edit the configuration file before starting
      --editor string               editor to use for edit e.g. vim, nano, code (default "$EDITOR" env var)
      --env stringToString          environment variables for the VM (default [])
  -f, --foreground                  Keep colima in the foreground
      --gateway-address ip          gateway address (default 192.168.5.2)
  -h, --help                        help for start
      --hostname string             custom hostname for the virtual machine
      --k3s-arg strings             additional args to pass to k3s (default [--disable=traefik])
      --k3s-listen-port int         k3s server listen port
  -k, --kubernetes                  start with Kubernetes
      --kubernetes-version string   must match a k3s version https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/releases (default "v1.35.0+k3s1")
  -m, --memory float32              memory in GiB (default 2)
      --model-runner string         AI model runner (docker, ramalama) (default "docker")
  -V, --mount strings               directories to mount, suffix ':w' for writable, disable with 'none'
      --mount-inotify               propagate inotify file events to the VM (default true)
      --mount-type string           volume driver for the mount (sshfs, 9p, virtiofs) (default "virtiofs")
  -z, --nested-virtualization       enable nested virtualization
      --network-address             assign reachable IP address to the VM
      --network-host-addresses      support port forwarding to specific host IP addresses
      --network-interface string    host network interface to use for bridged mode (default "en0")
      --network-mode string         network mode (shared, bridged) (default "shared")
      --network-preferred-route     use the assigned IP address as the preferred route for the VM (implies --network-address)
      --port-forwarder string       port forwarder to use (ssh, grpc, none) (default "ssh")
      --root-disk int               disk size in GiB for the root filesystem (default 20)
  -r, --runtime string              container runtime (incus, containerd, docker) (default "docker")
      --save-config                 persist and overwrite config file with (newly) specified flags (default true)
  -s, --ssh-agent                   forward SSH agent to the VM
      --ssh-config                  generate SSH config in ~/.ssh/config (default true)
      --ssh-port int                SSH server port
      --template                    use the template file for initial configuration (default true)
  -t, --vm-type string              virtual machine type (qemu, vz, krunkit) (default "vz")
      --vz-rosetta                  enable Rosetta for amd64 emulation

Global Flags:
  -p, --profile string   profile name, for multiple instances (default "default")
  -v, --verbose          enable verbose log
      --very-verbose     enable more verbose log
